n: Jeremiah, from the tribe of Benjamin, warns his kin to flee Jerusalem. Blow the trumpet in Tekoa and light a fire signal at Beth-haccerem—towns south of the city—because disaster is coming from the north. There’s a pun: Tekoa sounds like the Hebrew “blow” (tiq‘u).

f.g: A town about 10 miles south of Jerusalem; home of the prophet Amos.
“House of the vineyard,” a hill town near Jerusalem used for signal fires.

f.w: evil appeareth out of the north

n: Zion is like a lovely, delicate woman—or, as some translate, a pleasant pasture—about to be overrun.

f.g: Lovely, attractive.

n: Enemy kings, pictured as shepherds, will camp around her with their “flocks” (armies), each grazing his section bare.

f.g: A metaphor for foreign rulers and their troops.

n: The enemy speaks: “Get ready for battle! Let’s attack at noon!” Then, frustrated: “Too bad, the day is ending and the shadows are long.”

f.g: Literally “sanctify war”—armies performed religious rites before battle.

n: “Then let’s attack by night and destroy her palaces!” The enemy is relentless.
God Himself commands: cut down trees and build a siege ramp against Jerusalem. This city must be punished; it is full of oppression. The Babylonians built such ramps.

f.g: Build a siege ramp.

f.w: she is wholly oppression in the midst of her

n: As a well keeps its water fresh, Jerusalem keeps her wickedness flowing. Violence and destruction echo in her streets; sickness and wounds are always before God.

f.w: As a fountain casteth out her waters
f.g: As a well keeps its water flowing fresh.

n: Take warning, Jerusalem, or I will turn away from you in disgust and make you an empty wasteland. God still pleads.

f.w: lest my soul depart from thee

n: The enemy will glean Israel’s remnant thoroughly, like a grape picker passing his hand over the branches again and again to get every cluster.

f.g: Thoroughly pick over—gleaning means gathering what’s left after harvest.

n: Jeremiah asks: who will even listen to my warning? Their ears are “uncircumcised”—closed. God’s word offends them; they take no pleasure in it.

f.g: Closed, unresponsive—as if covered.

f.w: the word of the LORD is unto them a reproach

n: Jeremiah is full of the Lord’s anger and tired of holding it in. It will be poured out on children in the street, young men, husbands and wives, and the very old—no one exempt.

f.w: I am weary with holding in
him that is full of days
f.g: The very old.

n: Their houses, fields, and wives will be given to others when God stretches out His hand against the land—the curses of the covenant fulfilled.

f.w: their houses shall be turned unto others

n: From least to greatest, everyone is greedy for gain; from prophet to priest, everyone deals falsely. Corruption runs through the whole society.

f.w: every one is given to covetousness

n: They dress the people’s wound superficially, saying “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace. A key verse: false comfort that ignores the real problem only lets the wound fester.

f.w: Peace, peace; when there is no peace

f.g: Lightly, superficially.

n: Were they ashamed of their disgusting acts? Not at all—they didn’t even know how to blush. So they will fall with everyone else.
Stand at the crossroads and look; ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is, and walk in it—you’ll find rest for your souls. But they said, “We won’t.” Jesus echoes the promise of rest.

f.w: ye shall find rest for your souls

n: God posted watchmen—prophets—saying, “Listen for the trumpet!” But they replied, “We won’t listen.”
So God calls the nations as witnesses to see what will happen to His people.
Listen, earth: God will bring disaster on this people—the fruit of their own schemes—because they rejected His words and law.
Why bring Me imported frankincense from Sheba and fragrant cane from far away? Your offerings aren’t acceptable. Expensive worship can’t cover disobedience.

f.g: Frankincense from southern Arabia—a luxury import.

f.w: your burnt offerings are not acceptable

n: So God will put obstacles before them; fathers and sons, neighbors and friends will stumble and perish together.
A people is coming from the north—a great nation stirred up from the ends of the earth.

f.g: The farthest parts of the earth.

n: Armed with bow and spear, cruel and merciless, roaring like the sea, riding horses in battle formation against Zion.

f.w: they are cruel, and have no mercy

n: The people respond: we’ve heard the reports, and our hands hang limp; anguish grips us like a woman in labor.

f.w: as of a woman in travail

n: Don’t go out into the fields or walk the roads—the enemy’s sword is there, and terror is everywhere.

f.g: Hebrew magor missaviv—“terror all around,” a phrase Jeremiah repeats.

n: Put on sackcloth and roll in ashes; mourn bitterly as for an only son, for the destroyer will suddenly come.

f.g: Roll in ashes—an extreme sign of grief.

n: God tells Jeremiah: I have made you an assayer and tester among My people, to examine and test their ways—like someone testing metal.

f.g: Better: “an assayer and a tester” of metals.
Test their conduct, as metal is tested.

n: They are all hardened rebels, spreading slander—as hard as bronze and iron, and all corrupt.
A refining image: the bellows blow fiercely and the lead is consumed by fire, but the refining fails—the impurities won’t separate. Despite all efforts, the wicked aren’t removed.

f.g: The bellows blow hard (to heat the furnace).
The refiner smelts for nothing—the dross remains.

n: They’ll be called “rejected silver,” because the Lord has rejected them. Silver that can’t be purified is thrown away.

f.g: Rejected, worthless silver.
